limits.value: 10 minutes of wall clock on codeberg-medium, the largest runner, which is 4 CPU and 8G. codeberg-small is 5 minutes and codeberg-tiny is 2 minutes. Quoted: 'The specs are guidelines for how many resources builds are allowed to take at most, but we rely on "fair use".'

The RAM allocation counts filesystem writes against it: 'If your software uses 1 GB of RAM and wrote 1 GB of temporary files, it will be counted as 2 GB against the quota.' 2 GB of extra temp storage per container is granted.
The queue is shared and its fairness is enforced socially, not by a number: 'Don't jam the queue so other projects can also benefit from our offer.'
A '-lazy' variant of each runner trades latency for scheduling: 'We aim for completing the job within 24 hours'

record.limits_note: The 10-minute per-job ceiling on codeberg-medium binds first and it binds absolutely: no amount of queue patience makes a 30-minute job run. There is no published monthly allowance, so the ceiling is per job and the aggregate is fair use, which is a discretionary throttle rather than a quota.
record.binding_note: the 10-minute wall clock on the largest runner fails first and it fails hard: 4 vCPU for 10 minutes is 0.67 vCPU-hours per job, so a job that needs more than ten minutes cannot run at all however idle the queue is.

record.notes: The smallest compute ceiling in this class, and the record is worth keeping precisely because it is small: 0.67 vCPU-hours per job against GitHub's 24 vCPU-hours, a factor of 36. Two things make it worse than the arithmetic suggests. First, there is no published monthly allowance, so the aggregate is 'fair use', which is a discretionary throttle with no threshold to design against. Second, Codeberg's rules name the exact use comparative records exists to serve: 'No extensive pipelines to assist LLM-driven workflows'. That is a published-conditions question and it is vendor to judge, not this record's; what the record does is state the sentence. Not established: the egress term; whether the container is destroyed at job end (the 2 GB per-container temp storage grant implies it, but no sentence says so); and whether a job queued on a lazy runner counts against any aggregate at all, because no aggregate is published.

shape.note: codeberg-medium, the largest published runner: '4 | 8G | 10 min'. Disk is not published; the page grants '2 GB of additional storage for temporary files per container' and warns that filesystem writes count against the RAM allocation.

extras.price_arithmetic: USD 0.00, and no arithmetic is possible: there is no published monthly allowance. One job on codeberg-medium is 4 vCPU x 10 min = 0.67 vCPU-hours. The aggregate depends on how many jobs the fair-use policy tolerates, which is not a number and so cannot be multiplied.

session_cap.note: 10 minutes on codeberg-medium, 5 on small, 2 on tiny. A lazy variant may wait up to 24 hours for a slot. No monthly quota published.

concurrency.note: not published: no concurrent-job number appears on the page read. The queue is shared and governed by 'Don't jam the queue'.

keep_rate.basis: the container is per job; nothing is billed
